diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Diagnose edges as unsupported when they are not clearly grounded in the selected scenario and instead reflect a different causal branch.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When evidence supports multiple mechanisms, mark cross-mechanism links as unsupported edges instead of merging them into one pathway.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A node has no remaining supported function once its only causal connection is removed.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The primary diagnosis remains the unsupported edge; node removal is a secondary cleanup step because the node no longer contributes any evidence-grounded role in the retained pathway.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If a node participates only through an unsupported link and has no separate supported role, treat it as removable cleanup after the edge-level diagnosis.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose the core problem at the unsupported connection first, then remove any node left without an independent supported role.

diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose role-label errors separately from causal completeness problems.

diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When materials and properties are evidenced as part of ignition or consequence development, diagnose detached branches as underconnected rather than merely present.

diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If an edge looks too direct because a local mechanism is missing, diagnose the omission first and treat the edge as a shortcut created by that omission.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A supported operational step placed between two existing nodes should be represented explicitly rather than left implicit.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose omitted inspection, verification, or decision acts as missing intermediate steps when they are directly supported and causally local.

diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When diagnosing missing-step repairs, also check whether any surviving direct edge now improperly collapses the restored sequence.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A distinct internal process step between an input action and a reaction event was missing.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A local causal sequence was compressed between earlier failures and a downstream total-loss state.

diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If the evidence describes a continued intermediate state before a final failure, diagnose the gap as a missing step rather than treating the sequence as complete.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An upstream utility failure was linked directly to total loss even though temporary backup supply still existed.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: When a downstream loss occurs only after an intervening backup state, frame the problem as missing-step compression rather than immediate direct causation.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Do not diagnose total system loss as immediate if the record shows interim backup operation between the first failure and the final outage.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A partial redundancy failure was treated as if it were already complete loss of function.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If one backup train fails but another continues to operate, diagnose a staged degradation sequence rather than a direct transition to full loss.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When redundancy degrades in stages, diagnose each stage distinctly instead of collapsing partial loss into total failure.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A condition is asserted from text that does not directly describe that state variable.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A node is unsupported when the incident text does not directly establish the asserted condition as a distinct supported state.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If evidence describes who was affected or what happened, but not the claimed condition, diagnose unsupported condition semantics rather than a pathway gap.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A condition participates only downstream and lacks any incoming grounding link.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A condition lacking an incoming grounding connection is a disconnected-node problem.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a condition is only used downstream, diagnose missing grounding connectivity before diagnosing a missing step.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Terminal consequence semantics are disputed, but an explosion consequence is still supported.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If evidence still supports the endpoint phenomenon, diagnose it as semantic misalignment before diagnosing it as removable unsupported content.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Distinguish between a wrong consequence label and no supported consequence at all.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: The edge challenge was entirely dependent on the disputed terminal-node diagnosis.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A supported event node has no downstream causal participation.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A node with no supported downstream causal role is a disconnected observation and may be diagnosed as nonfunctional in the graph.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose dead-end observations as structural disconnects even when the report explicitly mentions them.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An incoming edge exists only to support a deleted dead-end observation.

diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If a node is removed for lacking downstream causal role, remove the incident edge that only serves that disconnected node.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: After diagnosing a node as disconnected, treat its feeder edge as graph cleanup rather than as a separate causal mechanism.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Repair/isolation state was misattached to leak creation instead of pressure buildup.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a local unsupported-edge problem: the condition affects retention and overpressure after leakage, not the origin of the leak path.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The no-venting repair state contributed to trapping and pressure buildup rather than to creation of the internal leak path.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a precursor changes what happens after leakage, diagnose it as pressure-buildup influence rather than leak causation.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Leak event had the wrong immediate cause attached.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The issue is best framed as unsupported attribution of a mechanism, because the narrative names a different physical cause for the leak path.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If the report attributes leakage to a specific physical defect, competing causes should not be attached to that leak event without separate evidence.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose wrongly attributed leak causes as unsupported edges, not as alternative parallel causes by default.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Descriptive service condition remained a terminal stub.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This is a disconnected-node issue, not an unsupported-node issue, because the condition is textually supported but not causally used.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Condition nodes that have only an incoming has edge and no downstream role do not function as meaningful causal conditions.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Treat isolated descriptive conditions as removable background unless the record supports a concrete downstream effect.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Retained equipment condition needed downstream integration into the release sequence.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The diagnosis is lack of causal integration for an otherwise valid condition node, not invalid node content.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Terminal condition nodes need evidence-supported downstream integration or removal.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a condition is well supported but isolated, diagnose the problem as missing integration rather than node invalidity.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Release-area condition needed integration into dispersion.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This indicates the condition was relevant, but only if framed as shaping the released cloud's behavior rather than left as standalone context.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Release-setting conditions should participate in the downstream mechanism they influence, such as dispersion.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose environmental condition nodes by asking which release or dispersion step they materially modify.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Support edge disappeared because its condition node was removed.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This implies the deleted condition was treated as nonessential background, so its attachment edge was cleanup rather than an independent causal issue.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: When a disconnected background condition lacks a strong downstream role and is deleted, its supporting attachment edge should also be removed.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If a node is deleted for lacking causal function, diagnose its remaining support edges as cleanup artifacts.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A material-detail node exists only inside an isolated composition subgraph.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a disconnected-node problem with an extraneous detail, not as a missing causal step in the accident sequence.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Nodes that do not participate in a valid supported path to the hazard function as isolated or dangling elements.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose isolated descriptive details as removable connectivity artifacts when they lack an independent causal role.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An equipment/entity node is present but not connected to the failure event involving that equipment.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The issue is best framed as poor integration of an existing node into the established event chain, rather than as absent accident content.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: An isolated composition subgraph that does not connect to the failure/propagation sequence is a disconnected-node issue.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a physical asset is isolated from its own failure event, diagnose the problem as missing integration into the main path.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A damage-evidence event appears as a terminal leaf despite evidence of later causal significance.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as an incomplete downstream linkage for an otherwise supported node, not as an unsupported extraction.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A dangling terminal node that does not lead to any further causal step indicates a connectivity defect.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If observed damage is supported but causally stranded, diagnose missing downstream linkage before considering node removal.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A leftover composition edge survives only as residue of an isolated side branch.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The diagnosis should treat such edges as part of the same disconnected-node cleanup, not as meaningful structure that deserves preservation.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Keeping an isolated composition edge preserves the disconnected subgraph rather than integrating the information into the main event chain.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose residual composition links as cleanup targets when they only maintain disconnected fragments.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Dead-end phase node duplicates entity semantics.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be framed as a low-severity duplicate-node issue, not as a missing causal step, because the retained graph already carries the same meaning through the material description.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: When a phase/state meaning is already embedded in another retained node and has no downstream role, diagnose it as redundant extraction.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose dead-end descriptive state nodes as redundancy when they do not change the causal story.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Phase node duplicates an existing release/dispersion progression.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This implies the issue is redundant semantic layering: the vapor state is already represented by retained release and dispersion events, so the extra condition node should not be treated as separate causal content.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If release and dispersion events already express the state transition, a separate state node with no added role is a duplicate-node diagnosis.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Prefer diagnosing duplicated state labels as redundancy when event structure already captures the same transformation.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Edge only supports a redundant endpoint node.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The edge is not an independent edge-quality problem; it is derivative of a duplicate-node diagnosis and should be framed as removable support for redundant extraction.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: When an attached node is redundant, incident edges that only serve that node inherit the redundancy diagnosis.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose node-dependent edges as derivative cleanup when they add no causal information beyond a redundant node.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Edge terminates at a duplicate state node already covered by retained events.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This suggests the correct diagnosis is redundant representation rather than a separate unsupported or weak-edge issue, because the retained event chain already conveys the relevant state change.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If an edge points only to a duplicated abstraction already expressed by retained causal events, frame it as redundant support rather than independent causal structure.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When event structure already encodes the meaning, diagnose extra supporting edges as redundancy, not as missing or weak causation.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: The graph was missing an upstream precursor material state before the initiating treatment action.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a missing-step problem centered on omitted pre-existing contents, not as a flaw in the downstream reaction-to-rupture chain.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Use a missing-step diagnosis when a supported upstream precursor is absent but is needed to explain formation of a later reactive state.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose untested or unknown initial contents as an omitted upstream precursor when they materially shape the later hazard.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A supported condition node existed but had no downstream causal role.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be framed as a disconnected-node issue: the condition itself is valid, but its role in the accident sequence was under-specified until tied to the relevant release step.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Treat a condition node as disconnected when it has no supported downstream connection into the accident progression.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a condition is evidenced but unused, diagnose missing connectivity before treating the node as unnecessary.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An over-specific ignition-source label was generalized while the ignition-source role was preserved.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The issue is best framed as uncertainty/schema handling, not as absence of an ignition-source concept.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If the report says the exact ignition source was not definitively identified, diagnose the problem as over-specific ignition-source modeling.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose named candidate ignition sources as a schema-mismatch problem when the evidence supports ignition occurrence but not source certainty.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A specific precursor activity was detached from an ignition source that remained uncertain.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The diagnostic problem is over-commitment of causation to one candidate precursor, not a missing causal step.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: When multiple ignition sources are possible, do not diagnose one upstream activity as the definitive generator of the ignition source.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Treat unjustified upstream anchoring of an uncertain ignition source as an over-specific diagnosis rather than as a connectivity gap.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: The ignition-source node stayed connected to the ignition event after being generalized.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The diagnosis should preserve the ignition function in the causal chain while relaxing only the source specificity.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Uncertain identification of the source does not remove the need to represent an ignition-source-to-ignition transition.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Do not diagnose uncertainty about source identity as permission to disconnect ignition causation from the ignition event.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A previously downstream-disconnected condition was given a supported mechanism role.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The issue is a participation gap for a condition node, which should be framed as a disconnected-node problem when evidence supports a downstream effect.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: If a condition node has no downstream causal use, diagnose it as disconnected unless it can be tied to an evidence-supported step.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a condition node is only descriptive and not mechanistic, diagnose a disconnected-node issue and seek a supported downstream link.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A documented propagation sequence was compressed into a single broader transition.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a missing intermediate step, not merely as a vague propagation edge.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Treat explicitly described local propagation stages as distinct missing-step issues when they are absent from the graph.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When the narrative separates two propagation stages, diagnose the omission as a missing step.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A direct causal edge bypassed a newly supported intermediate stage.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: Once the intermediate stage is recognized, the original direct link is best framed as a shortcut structure rather than a complete causal representation.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Do not keep a direct edge that skips over an explicitly supported intermediate event in the same causal chain.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If a direct edge survives only by skipping a documented step, diagnose the problem as structural compression.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A supported condition node had no downstream participation in the causal chain.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be framed as a disconnected-node issue where the condition is valid but under-integrated, not as an unsupported node problem.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: When a condition is supported by evidence but unused in the mechanism, diagnose it as disconnected and link it only to a supported downstream event.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: A supported condition without causal participation is a connectivity diagnosis, not a support diagnosis.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An inferred upstream state was modeled as a standalone causal condition without direct textual support.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed primarily as an unsupported-node problem, not as a missing step in the release-to-dispersion chain.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Treat inferred causal states without direct report support as unsupported nodes when the main event sequence is already represented.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose unsupported inferred conditions as evidence problems, not as gaps that must be preserved in the chain.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A causal edge depended entirely on a speculative upstream condition.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: Frame this as a derivative unsupported causal role created by the unsupported node, rather than as a separate sequencing or relation-type defect.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Do not elevate an edge to an independent diagnosis when its only problem is that it inherits unsupported causation from its source node.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When an edge is only invalid because its source node is unsupported, diagnose the core issue at the node level and treat the edge as consequential cleanup.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Independent accumulation-management failure was missing from the deposit pathway.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The accumulation problem should be diagnosed as incomplete because release alone does not explain why deposits remained and reached hazardous levels.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The graph omits the explicitly cited housekeeping contributor to hazardous accumulations.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When the source separately blames poor housekeeping for hazardous deposits, diagnose it as a missing causal step.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An apparent duplicate also served as the explicit ignition-stage representation.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: Duplicate-node diagnoses should be limited when one node preserves the ignition stage in the core explosion narrative.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The main causal sequence includes a distinct dust-cloud-to-ignition-to-explosion progression.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Do not frame every same-fact pair as removable duplication if one node captures a critical hazard stage such as ignition.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: The proposed direct link was conditional on removing an intermediate ignition node.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This is not an independent missing-edge diagnosis; it only becomes relevant under an alternative node structure where the ignition-stage node is removed.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A direct replacement edge is only warranted after the duplicate ignition-source node is removed.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Distinguish true missing edges from contingent replacement edges that only apply if the graph is restructured first.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A condition node was a dead end relative to the accumulation event.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The disconnected-node issue is best framed as missing participation of material state in the event where deposited material actually accumulates.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The material/property subgraph was not integrated into the operative causal chain, and the condition nodes had no outgoing role.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When a material-condition node has no downstream use, diagnose where that condition becomes operational in the event chain.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A fuel-property node was disconnected from the propagation event it powers.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The isolation of combustibility should be diagnosed as missing functional linkage to the explosion event, not as a problem with the property label itself.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The material/property subgraph was not integrated into the operative causal chain.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If a fuel property is stranded, diagnose the event where that property is actually consumed as explosion fuel.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Redundancy was handled at the edge level instead of by deleting a node.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The duplicate-mechanism concern can be framed as over-connection between near-equivalent local nodes even when both semantic labels are retained.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Remove the edge that exists only because of the redundant local duplication.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If reviewers keep both nodes for semantic clarity, diagnose and prune only the redundant bridging edge.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A key process event ends without any path into ignition or loss.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a broken main accident chain, not as an isolated ignition event.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A key event that has no outgoing connection to the ignition/explosion sequence is a disconnected-node problem.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If a central pre-loss event does not feed the final outcome, diagnose missing chain continuity before searching for new content.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: An existing node partially captures the missing circumstance but is framed too narrowly.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a missing-step framing issue that can be resolved by recasting an existing node, not necessarily by adding a new one.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The missing causal circumstance can be made explicit by reusing an existing node to represent it.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When evidence supports a broader causal reading of an existing node, diagnose the gap as weak framing of a missing step rather than missing extraction.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: A documented contextual circumstance exists in the graph but does not participate in causation.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as an omitted causal link for an existing circumstance, rather than as absent evidence or absent nodes.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A causal circumstance that is already present but not connected leaves the major causal step effectively absent.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If a supporting circumstance node is present but idle, diagnose the issue as missing integration into the chain.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: The consequence meaning is correct, but the node label violates the schema.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: This should be diagnosed as a schema-mismatch issue, not as a content-selection error.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The hazard consequence node should use the required generic label, while the specific consequence stays in the name field.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Separate schema violations from causal-content problems; a correct concept in the wrong field is a schema diagnosis.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Initiating event is underspecified.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The issue is best framed as a missing initiating mechanism within an existing event, not as a separate new branch.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: The explicit operator misidentification mechanism is missing from the initiation sequence.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose omitted belief, indication, or position-reading details as missing-step refinement when they explain why an existing initiating event occurred.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Event type does not match evidence semantics.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The problem is a schema-mismatch diagnosis about event classification rather than a missing-causality problem.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: A sudden loss of containment should be classified with the schema-preferred instantaneous release type.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: When the sequence is intact but the event label conflicts with report wording, frame the issue as schema mismatch.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Condition node has no downstream causal role.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The issue should be diagnosed as disconnected-node cleanup: the condition is supported, but it remains only descriptive until linked into the release sequence.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Supported condition nodes should participate downstream in the causal chain rather than remain attribute-only descriptors.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: Diagnose supported-but-stranded conditions as connectivity problems, not unsupported nodes.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Process condition is stranded as an attribute.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The temperature issue is best framed as missing downstream participation for a retained condition node, not as a need to delete the node.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Several condition nodes lack downstream participation in the causal chain.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: If a condition is evidenced and relevant, diagnose the problem as missing connectivity before considering removal.

diagnosis_patterns.observed_pattern: Hazard-relevant material property is disconnected from the consequence.
diagnosis_patterns.diagnosis_interpretation: The combustibility issue is a diagnosis of missing consequence linkage for an otherwise supported condition node.
diagnosis_patterns.supporting_rule: Connect retained hazard conditions to the event or consequence they materially enable when evidence shows participation.
diagnosis_patterns.few_shot_takeaway: For fire scenarios, diagnose disconnected combustibility or flammability nodes as missing links to the fire consequence.

planning.takeaway: If a link imports causation from a different scenario than the pathway being modeled, delete the edge rather than weakening the whole chain.
When a node becomes orphaned after supported edge cleanup and adds no independent pathway role, remove it as minimal graph cleanup.
Accept relabels that fix schema-role mismatch without changing the supported causal sequence.
Accept connectivity fixes that integrate a supported detached branch into the main chain without creating a shortcut.
Accept minimal connectivity fixes that integrate an underconnected material branch into an already valid causal sequence without adding new nodes.
When evidence shows barrier failure or local exposure precedes damage, add that intermediate event instead of linking the material straight to the damage mechanism.
If a direct edge skips an evidenced local mechanism, delete the shortcut edge once the intermediate step is inserted.
If diagnosis finds a supported human or operational action missing from an otherwise correct physical sequence, add it as a local intermediate event.
When a new local step is added, also prune the old bypass edge so the graph reflects the supported causal sequence rather than both the sequence and its shortcut.
When the report explicitly describes an internal transition that explains why a later event occurred, represent it as its own node instead of collapsing it into adjacent events.
If a new intermediate node makes an older direct link a shortcut, remove the shortcut so the graph reflects the full supported mechanism.
When a node is semantically correct but structurally mislabeled, prefer a label fix over replacing the node or changing its meaning.
When the record shows a specific last-step transition before full system loss, preserve it as its own event rather than collapsing the sequence.
If backup power continues after a primary power failure, do not keep a direct edge that implies immediate total power loss.
When one redundant source fails but another still operates, model staged degradation and avoid direct links to full loss.
Accept deletion of speculative condition nodes when the evidence supports exposure or outcome but not the asserted condition itself.
Accept the smallest edge addition that restores grounding for an under-integrated condition instead of expanding the graph with new nodes.
Accept removal of edges that rely entirely on an unsupported node to keep the graph evidence-grounded.
If the endpoint is semantically imperfect but still represents the supported accident consequence, keep it rather than deleting the graph’s only hazard outcome.
When a node-deletion proposal is rejected, reject dependent edge removals unless there is an independent edge-level diagnosis.
A factually supported event can still be removed if it only serves as a dead-end observation and does not advance the causal chain.
Clean up edges attached solely to a deleted disconnected node.
Fix unsupported causation by rerouting the edge to the specific downstream mechanism the evidence actually supports.
If the narrative assigns a leak path to a different physical cause, remove the unsupported upstream edge.
Delete terminal condition stubs instead of forcing weak causal links.
If a condition is kept, connect it to the nearest downstream event it materially shapes.
Use environmental condition nodes only when they are integrated into a supported release or dispersion mechanism.
After deleting a nonfunctional node, also delete the attachment edges that only existed to support it.
If a material-detail node does not contribute its own supported causal step, prefer deleting it rather than keeping an isolated side branch.
When an equipment node is stranded outside the main path, reconnect it to the specific failure event already supported by the narrative.
If a failure-evidence node ends the chain prematurely, connect it to the next supported event instead of leaving it as a terminal leaf.
After deleting an unsupported standalone node, also remove any leftover composition edge that would keep the disconnected fragment alive.
If a state node is a dead-end restatement of an entity's basic description, remove it rather than keeping duplicate semantics.
Do not keep a standalone condition node for a state that is already adequately represented by retained process events.
When a node is correctly removed as redundant, also remove incident edges that have no remaining independent function.
If an edge only feeds a duplicate state abstraction, delete the edge with the redundant node instead of preserving both.
When a report supports unknown pre-existing contents as part of the hazard mechanism, add that upstream material state rather than leaving the chain to begin at the treatment step.
If a condition node is valid but isolated, attach it to the specific release or reaction step it helps enable.
If the report confirms ignition but not the exact source, generalize the ignition-source node instead of committing the graph to one candidate source.
Delete upstream links that force an uncertain ignition source into a single specific pathway unsupported by the report.
Do not remove a required ignition-source-to-ignition link just because the ignition source has been renamed to reflect uncertainty.
When a condition node is causally unused, add the most directly supported downstream connection that gives it an active role in the mechanism.
When a report names a separate propagation stage, represent it as its own event node rather than folding it into a downstream consequence.
If a direct link skips over a documented intermediate event, delete the shortcut edge after inserting the missing step.
Do not leave supported condition nodes isolated; attach them to a concrete downstream event if the evidence supports a causal contribution.
If a condition is only inferred from equipment type or naming and is not directly supported by the report, remove it rather than treating it as a causal step.
When a source node is speculative, remove any edge that turns that speculation into asserted causation.
When hazardous deposits are attributed to both release and failure to remove material, model housekeeping as its own causal step.
Treat apparent duplicates cautiously if one node carries a necessary ignition-stage role in the hazard sequence.
If an intermediate node is retained, avoid adding a bypass edge that only existed to replace it.
Use downstream links from condition nodes to integrate isolated material-property subgraphs into the main accident chain.
When combustibility is isolated, connect it to the explosion step it makes possible.
If two nearby nodes express nearly the same local fact, pruning the connecting edge can reduce redundancy even when both nodes stay.
When a key process event is a dead end just before the loss event, add the minimal downstream edge that reconnects the main sequence.
If the graph already contains the right physical element but names it too narrowly, prefer a rename that captures the causal circumstance over creating another node.
When an evidence-backed circumstance node already exists but is not in the chain, connect it to the affected event rather than adding parallel structure.
Fix schema-only node errors with a relabel, without changing the underlying consequence meaning.
Prefer a precise rename over a new node when the omitted mechanism is a more specific explanation of an existing event.
Correct event typing when the evidence clearly describes a sudden release rather than an ongoing discharge.
When a condition is evidenced as part of the loss event, connect it downstream instead of leaving it only as a material attribute.
Give supported process conditions a causal role when they are currently disconnected from the event chain.
Tie combustible or flammable properties to the fire consequence when they are otherwise left disconnected.

diagnosis.takeaway: When evidence supports multiple mechanisms, mark cross-mechanism links as unsupported edges instead of merging them into one pathway.
Diagnose the core problem at the unsupported connection first, then remove any node left without an independent supported role.
Diagnose role-label errors separately from causal completeness problems.
When materials and properties are evidenced as part of ignition or consequence development, diagnose detached branches as underconnected rather than merely present.
Diagnose isolated material/property branches as disconnected-node issues when the main accident progression is already represented.
Diagnose material-to-degradation gaps as missing-step problems when evidence identifies a specific exposure or barrier-failure event.
If an edge looks too direct because a local mechanism is missing, diagnose the omission first and treat the edge as a shortcut created by that omission.
Diagnose omitted inspection, verification, or decision acts as missing intermediate steps when they are directly supported and causally local.
When diagnosing missing-step repairs, also check whether any surviving direct edge now improperly collapses the restored sequence.
Diagnose a missing-step problem when the source gives a separate mechanism-bearing transition that changes the state of the system before the next event.
When a direct edge only exists because an intermediate mechanism was omitted, diagnose the omission first and treat the edge as a shortcut artifact.
If the content is right but the field value violates the schema, diagnose it as schema mismatch rather than as a substantive causal-model error.
If the evidence describes a continued intermediate state before a final failure, diagnose the gap as a missing step rather than treating the sequence as complete.
Do not diagnose total system loss as immediate if the record shows interim backup operation between the first failure and the final outage.
When redundancy degrades in stages, diagnose each stage distinctly instead of collapsing partial loss into total failure.
If evidence describes who was affected or what happened, but not the claimed condition, diagnose unsupported condition semantics rather than a pathway gap.
When a condition is only used downstream, diagnose missing grounding connectivity before diagnosing a missing step.
If an edge becomes invalid only because its source node is unsupported, diagnose the node first and treat the edge as secondary cleanup.
Distinguish between a wrong consequence label and no supported consequence at all.
Resolve node validity before escalating attached-edge deletions that have no stand-alone diagnostic basis.
Diagnose dead-end observations as structural disconnects even when the report explicitly mentions them.
After diagnosing a node as disconnected, treat its feeder edge as graph cleanup rather than as a separate causal mechanism.
When a precursor changes what happens after leakage, diagnose it as pressure-buildup influence rather than leak causation.
Diagnose wrongly attributed leak causes as unsupported edges, not as alternative parallel causes by default.
Treat isolated descriptive conditions as removable background unless the record supports a concrete downstream effect.
When a condition is well supported but isolated, diagnose the problem as missing integration rather than node invalidity.
Diagnose environmental condition nodes by asking which release or dispersion step they materially modify.
If a node is deleted for lacking causal function, diagnose its remaining support edges as cleanup artifacts.
Diagnose isolated descriptive details as removable connectivity artifacts when they lack an independent causal role.
When a physical asset is isolated from its own failure event, diagnose the problem as missing integration into the main path.
If observed damage is supported but causally stranded, diagnose missing downstream linkage before considering node removal.
Diagnose residual composition links as cleanup targets when they only maintain disconnected fragments.
Diagnose dead-end descriptive state nodes as redundancy when they do not change the causal story.
Prefer diagnosing duplicated state labels as redundancy when event structure already captures the same transformation.
Diagnose node-dependent edges as derivative cleanup when they add no causal information beyond a redundant node.
When event structure already encodes the meaning, diagnose extra supporting edges as redundancy, not as missing or weak causation.
Diagnose untested or unknown initial contents as an omitted upstream precursor when they materially shape the later hazard.
When a condition is evidenced but unused, diagnose missing connectivity before treating the node as unnecessary.
Diagnose named candidate ignition sources as a schema-mismatch problem when the evidence supports ignition occurrence but not source certainty.
Treat unjustified upstream anchoring of an uncertain ignition source as an over-specific diagnosis rather than as a connectivity gap.
Do not diagnose uncertainty about source identity as permission to disconnect ignition causation from the ignition event.
When a condition node is only descriptive and not mechanistic, diagnose a disconnected-node issue and seek a supported downstream link.
When the narrative separates two propagation stages, diagnose the omission as a missing step.
If a direct edge survives only by skipping a documented step, diagnose the problem as structural compression.
A supported condition without causal participation is a connectivity diagnosis, not a support diagnosis.
Diagnose unsupported inferred conditions as evidence problems, not as gaps that must be preserved in the chain.
When an edge is only invalid because its source node is unsupported, diagnose the core issue at the node level and treat the edge as consequential cleanup.
When the source separately blames poor housekeeping for hazardous deposits, diagnose it as a missing causal step.
Do not frame every same-fact pair as removable duplication if one node captures a critical hazard stage such as ignition.
Distinguish true missing edges from contingent replacement edges that only apply if the graph is restructured first.
When a material-condition node has no downstream use, diagnose where that condition becomes operational in the event chain.
If a fuel property is stranded, diagnose the event where that property is actually consumed as explosion fuel.
If reviewers keep both nodes for semantic clarity, diagnose and prune only the redundant bridging edge.
If a central pre-loss event does not feed the final outcome, diagnose missing chain continuity before searching for new content.
When evidence supports a broader causal reading of an existing node, diagnose the gap as weak framing of a missing step rather than missing extraction.
If a supporting circumstance node is present but idle, diagnose the issue as missing integration into the chain.
Separate schema violations from causal-content problems; a correct concept in the wrong field is a schema diagnosis.
Diagnose omitted belief, indication, or position-reading details as missing-step refinement when they explain why an existing initiating event occurred.
When the sequence is intact but the event label conflicts with report wording, frame the issue as schema mismatch.
Diagnose supported-but-stranded conditions as connectivity problems, not unsupported nodes.
If a condition is evidenced and relevant, diagnose the problem as missing connectivity before considering removal.
For fire scenarios, diagnose disconnected combustibility or flammability nodes as missing links to the fire consequence.

planning_matched_rules.rule: Condition nodes should not remain stranded descriptors; add downstream causal links when the condition participates in the accident sequence.
Remove an edge when it is not clearly supported within the selected causal pathway and instead mixes in a separate alternative mechanism.
After an unsupported edge is removed, delete a node if that node only participated through that link and has no other evidence-grounded role in the selected pathway.
When evidence describes ignition occurring as a step in the sequence, classify it as an event/mechanism rather than as a separate ignition-energy source.
Add a link from a detached material-property branch to the documented ignition step when evidence supports it and the link does not bypass an existing intermediate step.
When a material/condition branch is disconnected from the main release chain, add the minimal edge that reconnects it to the existing release event.
Insert a missing local causal step when diagnosis shows the graph jumps directly from material presence to degradation onset.
Remove a direct causal edge when it compresses a diagnosed missing intermediate mechanism and should be replaced by a more local chain.
When the report identifies a distinct supported operational step between existing nodes, add that missing intermediate step explicitly.
After inserting a supported intermediate step, remove any direct edge that becomes an overly direct shortcut around it.
Add the smallest evidence-grounded intermediate step when the source describes a distinct process transition between an upstream action and a downstream reaction.
Delete a direct causal edge when a supported intermediate step lies between the same endpoints; keeping the direct link preserves the omission.
Correct schema-only label mismatches while preserving the existing node meaning.
Add a documented intermediate event when the graph omits the immediate precursor between upstream failures and a downstream loss state.
Remove a direct edge that bypasses a documented temporary backup state after an initial utility failure.
Remove a direct edge that collapses partial backup degradation into complete functional loss when another backup source remained active.
Remove a condition node when the cited evidence does not directly establish that condition as a distinct supported state.
Add a minimal grounding edge when a condition node is otherwise disconnected from supported upstream context.
When a supporting condition is not distinctly supported, remove its dependent causal edge as well.
Do not delete the only terminal hazard node when the evidence still supports a real consequence and the issue is mainly mechanism or label alignment.
Do not remove an attachment edge when its deletion was justified only by deletion of a node that is being retained.
Remove supported but disconnected observations when they have no distinct downstream causal role.
When deleting a dead-end node, also remove incident edges that only feed that deleted observation.
When evidence shows a state affects pressure retention rather than leak formation, reconnect it to the pressure-buildup step.
Delete edges that contradict the locally stated mechanism for how a leak path formed.
Remove disconnected background conditions when no distinct downstream causal role is supported.
Retained condition nodes should gain an evidence-backed downstream link or be removed.
Retained release-environment conditions should be linked to the step they influence, such as dispersion.
When a disconnected condition node is removed, remove its dependent support edge as cleanup.
Remove a standalone node when it lacks a separate evidence-grounded causal role and only preserves a disconnected subgraph.
Integrate an isolated equipment/entity node by linking it to the supported failure event it participates in.
Give a dangling damage or observation node a supported downstream role when evidence ties it to an existing causal step.
Remove a composition edge when its only effect is to preserve an isolated subgraph after the dependent node is deleted.
Delete a condition node when it only restates information already embedded in another retained node and adds no independent causal role.
Delete a condition node when its meaning is already carried by an existing release-to-dispersion event chain and it adds no separate causal value.
Remove an edge that exists only to support a redundant node slated for deletion.
Remove an edge that points only to a redundant state node whose meaning is already captured elsewhere in the retained causal sequence.
Add a supported upstream precursor when diagnosis shows the graph starts too late and omits a material state needed to explain a later hazardous mixture.
Connect a supported condition node to the downstream event it enables when diagnosis shows the condition is otherwise disconnected from the accident logic.
When the exact ignition source is not definitively identified, model it as an uncertain ignition-source node rather than a specific mechanism.
Do not anchor an uncertain ignition source to one specific upstream activity when the evidence lists multiple possible sources.
After generalizing an uncertain ignition source, retain a generic causal link from the ignition-source node to the ignition event.
A condition node that is disconnected downstream should be linked to an evidence-supported mechanism step or else removed.
Add an intermediate node when the source material explicitly describes a distinct causal step that is currently collapsed into a broader transition.
Remove a direct edge when an explicitly supported intermediate step should sit between the same source and target.
Connect a supported but disconnected condition node to a supported downstream event when that gives the condition an explicit causal role.
Delete inferred upstream condition nodes when the incident description does not directly establish that state as a confirmed cause and the supported causal sequence remains intact without it.
Delete causal edges that make an unsupported inferred condition a direct cause of an event when that causation is not established by the incident description.
Add an explicit missing step when the source identifies a separate contributor that allowed hazardous accumulations to persist.
Do not delete a supported node when it preserves the explicit ignition stage in an ignition-triggered explosion chain.
Do not add a direct replacement edge when its justification depends on a node deletion that was not approved.
Connect disconnected condition nodes to the operative event they enable when they otherwise remain dead ends.
Link a fuel-property condition to the explosion event where that property is functionally used as fuel.
Remove an edge that exists only to support a redundant local duplication and is not needed for the retained chain structure.
Restore a broken downstream chain by linking the accumulated hazardous state to the ignition event.
Reuse an existing node to represent a missing causal circumstance when the evidence supports it, instead of adding a new node.
Make an already extracted causal circumstance explicit by connecting it to the event it enables.
Hazard consequence nodes should use the schema label, with the specific consequence kept in the name field.
If an explicit initiating mechanism is missing, refine the existing event node to capture it with minimal graph change.
Use the schema label that matches the cited event semantics; a sudden loss of containment should be typed as instantaneous.
Connect a condition node to the consequence it materially enables when ignition-and-burning evidence supports that role.

If a node participates only through an unsupported link and has no separate supported role, treat it as removable cleanup after the edge-level diagnosis.
Treat a node as schema-mismatched when its evidence describes the ignition event itself rather than a distinct source of ignition energy.
Treat detached material/property subgraphs as connectivity defects when they do not feed the documented release-ignition-consequence chain.
If a material/phase branch has no outgoing connection into the accident sequence, frame it as disconnected-node underconnectivity.
The diagnosed issue is an omitted upstream exposure or protection-failure step preceding crack initiation.
When a direct edge is compressed because an upstream mechanism is absent, capture the problem as a missing step rather than as a separate unsupported-edge issue.
A supported operational step placed between two existing nodes should be represented explicitly rather than left implicit.
If a direct link bypasses a newly restored supported step, treat the direct link as overly direct and remove it.
The graph skips a supported in-system poor-dilution/poor-mixing overconcentration step between feed entry and decomposition.
The main connectivity problem is better characterized as a missing causal step rather than a separate weak-edge issue.
The hazard consequence node uses the hazard name as its label instead of the schema-required label HazardConsequence.
Diagnose a documented omitted immediate precursor as a missing-step problem when the narrative shows an intervening operating state before the final loss.
When a downstream loss occurs only after an intervening backup state, frame the problem as missing-step compression rather than immediate direct causation.
If one backup train fails but another continues to operate, diagnose a staged degradation sequence rather than a direct transition to full loss.
A node is unsupported when the incident text does not directly establish the asserted condition as a distinct supported state.
A condition lacking an incoming grounding connection is a disconnected-node problem.
No separate unsupported-edge diagnosis is needed when the edge problem follows from a speculative source condition.
If evidence still supports the endpoint phenomenon, diagnose it as semantic misalignment before diagnosing it as removable unsupported content.
Do not diagnose a dependent edge as separately removable when its only problem comes from a node diagnosis that is not accepted.
A node with no supported downstream causal role is a disconnected observation and may be diagnosed as nonfunctional in the graph.
If a node is removed for lacking downstream causal role, remove the incident edge that only serves that disconnected node.
The no-venting repair state contributed to trapping and pressure buildup rather than to creation of the internal leak path.
If the report attributes leakage to a specific physical defect, competing causes should not be attached to that leak event without separate evidence.
Condition nodes that have only an incoming has edge and no downstream role do not function as meaningful causal conditions.
Terminal condition nodes need evidence-supported downstream integration or removal.
Release-setting conditions should participate in the downstream mechanism they influence, such as dispersion.
When a disconnected background condition lacks a strong downstream role and is deleted, its supporting attachment edge should also be removed.
Nodes that do not participate in a valid supported path to the hazard function as isolated or dangling elements.
An isolated composition subgraph that does not connect to the failure/propagation sequence is a disconnected-node issue.
A dangling terminal node that does not lead to any further causal step indicates a connectivity defect.
Keeping an isolated composition edge preserves the disconnected subgraph rather than integrating the information into the main event chain.
When a phase/state meaning is already embedded in another retained node and has no downstream role, diagnose it as redundant extraction.
If release and dispersion events already express the state transition, a separate state node with no added role is a duplicate-node diagnosis.
When an attached node is redundant, incident edges that only serve that node inherit the redundancy diagnosis.
If an edge points only to a duplicated abstraction already expressed by retained causal events, frame it as redundant support rather than independent causal structure.
Use a missing-step diagnosis when a supported upstream precursor is absent but is needed to explain formation of a later reactive state.
Treat a condition node as disconnected when it has no supported downstream connection into the accident progression.
If the report says the exact ignition source was not definitively identified, diagnose the problem as over-specific ignition-source modeling.
When multiple ignition sources are possible, do not diagnose one upstream activity as the definitive generator of the ignition source.
Uncertain identification of the source does not remove the need to represent an ignition-source-to-ignition transition.
If a condition node has no downstream causal use, diagnose it as disconnected unless it can be tied to an evidence-supported step.
Treat explicitly described local propagation stages as distinct missing-step issues when they are absent from the graph.
Do not keep a direct edge that skips over an explicitly supported intermediate event in the same causal chain.
When a condition is supported by evidence but unused in the mechanism, diagnose it as disconnected and link it only to a supported downstream event.
Treat inferred causal states without direct report support as unsupported nodes when the main event sequence is already represented.
Do not elevate an edge to an independent diagnosis when its only problem is that it inherits unsupported causation from its source node.

The material/property subgraph was not integrated into the operative causal chain.
